items.q: If you collect 10 class heights, what type of variable is this?
hints: Think about whether height can take any value within a range, or only whole-number counts.
Height can be measured to any level of precision (e.g. 152.3 cm), so it's not restricted to whole counts.
Continuous

items.q: Give one primary and one secondary data source.
hints: Primary data is collected first-hand; secondary data already exists from another source.
A survey you run yourself is primary; a dataset someone else already published is secondary.
Survey and published dataset

items.q: State one risk of a small sample size.
hints: Think about whether a small group can reliably reflect the whole population.
With few data points, unusual results have a bigger effect on the overall picture.
It may be less representative

items.a: Data from every member of the population
hints: Compare a census to a sample.
A census surveys everyone, not just a subset.
Data from every member of the population
Compare a sample to a census.
A sample only surveys part of the population, not everyone.
A subset of the population

items.q: Why might bias be a problem in data collection?
hints: Think about what happens if the data collected doesn't fairly represent the whole population.
Biased data skews the conclusions away from the true picture.
It can distort the results

items.q: Which data set is more spread out: range 8 or range 14?
hints: A larger range means the data is more spread out.
14 is greater than 8.
Range 14

items.q: Which is more spread out: IQR 6 or IQR 11?
hints: A larger interquartile range means the middle 50% of the data is more spread out.
11 is greater than 6.
IQR 11

items.q: For classes 0-10, 10-20, 20-30, find the class midpoints.
hints: The midpoint of a class is halfway between its endpoints.

items.q: A grouped table has midpoints 5, 15, 25 with frequencies 3, 5, 2. Estimate the mean.
hints: Multiply each midpoint by its frequency, sum these, then divide by the total frequency.

items.q: Why is a grouped mean estimated rather than exact?
items.a: Exact values inside each class are unknown
hints: Think about what information is lost when data is grouped into classes.
We only know how many values fall in each class, not their exact values, so the midpoint is used as a stand-in.
Exact values inside each class are unknown

items.q: For classes 20-30, 30-40, 40-50, find the class midpoints.
hints: The midpoint of a class is halfway between its endpoints.

items.q: A grouped table has midpoints 10, 20, 30 with frequencies 2, 4, 4. Estimate the mean.
hints: Multiply each midpoint by its frequency, sum these, then divide by the total frequency.
Recall the formula used for the y-axis of a histogram.
Frequency density = frequency / class width.
Frequency divided by class width
